title: “IF YOUR EYE CAUSES YOU TO SIN, TEAR IT OUT” — WAS JESUS BEING LITERAL?
paragraphs: “IF YOUR EYE CAUSES YOU TO SIN, TEAR IT OUT” — WAS JESUS BEING LITERAL?
The terrifying words of Jesus were never permission to destroy your body. They were a warning not to make peace with the sin destroying your soul.
There are verses people underline because they comfort them.
There are verses they put on coffee mugs.
And then there are the words of Jesus that make you stop reading.
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
What do you do with that?
Because Jesus did not whisper it.
He did not apologize for it.
And He did not soften it with, “But don’t take this too seriously.”
He said it in the middle of one of the most famous sermons ever preached.
And maybe the most disturbing thing about the sentence is not the image of losing an eye.
Maybe it is the possibility that Jesus knows how desperately we protect the things that are killing us.
Read His words in context.

In Matthew 5:27–30, Jesus turns from the outward act of adultery to the inward world of desire. He teaches that obedience to God cannot be reduced to maintaining a respectable exterior while secretly cultivating lust within.
Then comes the shocking language.
The Greek of Matthew 5:29 begins:
Εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ὁ δεξιὸς σκανδαλίζει σε, ἔξελε αὐτὸν καὶ βάλε ἀπὸ σοῦ…
Ei de ho ophthalmos sou ho dexios skandalizei se, exele auton kai bale apo sou…
A close rendering is:
“And if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you…”
Then Jesus continues with the reason: it is better to lose one member than for the whole person to be thrown into Gehenna.
A few words matter enormously here.
The verb translated “causes you to sin” or “causes you to stumble” is σκανδαλίζει — skandalizei, from σκανδαλίζω — skandalizō.
It carries the idea of causing someone to stumble, fall, or be entrapped.
It is related to the word from which English eventually gets “scandal,” although reading the modern English meaning of “scandal” directly back into every New Testament occurrence would be misleading.
Jesus is talking about something that becomes an occasion for spiritual falling.
Something that keeps pulling you toward rebellion.
Something precious enough that you keep defending it even while it keeps dragging you away from God.
And then Jesus says:
ἔξελε αὐτόν — exele auton.
Take it out.
Remove it.
The language is deliberately violent.
But was Jesus commanding His followers to mutilate themselves?
The context strongly points in another direction.
Jesus had just relocated the moral battlefield from merely outward behavior to the heart.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’”
Then Jesus goes deeper.
The problem is not solved simply because your hands have remained technically innocent while your inner life has become a sanctuary for deliberate lust.
That matters because removing an eye would not remove lust from the human heart.
A blind person can lust.
Removing a hand would not remove greed.
A person without hands can covet.
Cutting flesh cannot perform surgery on the sinful desires of the heart.
And Jesus Himself later teaches that evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery and other sins proceed from within, out of the human heart (Mark 7:20–23).
So no, the point is not self-mutilation.
But do not breathe too easily yet.
Because once we recognize the forceful imagery, there is a temptation to domesticate it.
“Oh. It’s figurative.”
And then we move on.
As though “figurative” means “not serious.”
It does not.
Jesus uses shocking, hyperbolic imagery to communicate the deadly seriousness of sin and the radical response discipleship may require.
The command is not:
Destroy your body.
The command is closer to:
Stop negotiating with whatever repeatedly leads you into sin.
And suddenly the verse gets personal.
Because almost everyone has an “eye.”
Something you keep looking at.
Something you keep returning to.
Something you know awakens desires you should not feed.
Maybe it really is what your eyes consume.
The account you refuse to unfollow.
The conversation you keep reopening.
The private browser.
The messages you delete.
The relationship everyone thinks is innocent.
The fantasy you entertain because nobody else can see it.
The resentment you rehearse in bed.
The money you cannot stop worshiping.
The approval you need so badly that you will compromise your convictions to keep receiving it.
The bitterness you call discernment.
The pride you call confidence.
The gossip you disguise as concern.
The addiction you have renamed a coping mechanism.
The secret you have protected longer than you have protected your intimacy with Christ.
You keep saying:
“I can handle it.”
Jesus says:
“If it causes you to stumble…”
You say:
“I know when to stop.”
Jesus says:
“Throw it away.”
You say:
“But I need it.”
And Jesus forces the question you were hoping Christianity would never ask:
Do you need it more than you want holiness?
That hurts.
Because sometimes we want Jesus to forgive the sin we have no intention of abandoning.
We want grace without surrender.
Mercy without repentance.
A Savior who removes guilt without touching our idols.
But that is not the Jesus speaking in Matthew 5.
The Jesus who saves sinners is also the Jesus who calls sinners to repentance.
And repentance is not self-hatred.
Repentance is not paying God back.
Repentance is not punishing your body until God decides you have suffered enough.
The Greek New Testament commonly uses μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance: a turning of mind and orientation that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Grace does not teach us to become casual about sin.
Grace gives us somewhere to run when sin has exposed us.
And this is where the story changes.
Because perhaps you have already failed.
Maybe you are reading this after promising God for the hundredth time that you would never go back.
Then you went back.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your church does not know.
Your friends see the worship songs you share but not the war you fight when the room gets quiet.
You know how to say, “God is good.”
But inside you are wondering:
Would God still want me if people knew what I have become?
Look at Jesus.
Not at your record.
Not at your shame.
Look at Him.
The Gospel does not announce that good people finally learned how to behave.
The Gospel announces that sinners who could not rescue themselves were loved by a Savior who came to rescue them.
Christ did not come merely to make scandalous people more respectable.
He came to redeem sinners.
The cross is where the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God meet without either one being minimized.
Sin is so serious that Christians cannot shrug at Calvary.
Grace is so astonishing that Christians cannot look at Calvary and conclude that repentant sinners are beyond redemption.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And forgiveness is not purchased by tearing out your eye.
It was purchased at immeasurable cost by Christ.
You do not mutilate yourself to become worthy of grace.
You come to Christ empty-handed.
Then, because His grace is real, you begin cutting away what keeps pulling you back toward the grave He rescued you from.
That may mean deleting something.
Blocking someone.
Confessing to someone trustworthy.
Ending an immoral relationship.
Moving the computer out of the bedroom.
Giving someone accountability.
Walking away from money you cannot receive honestly.
Leaving environments where your sobriety, fidelity, integrity, or obedience continually collapses.
Surrendering access.
Changing routines.
Admitting that what is “not technically sinful” for somebody else has become spiritually disastrous for you.
Not because those actions earn salvation.
They do not.
But sometimes repentance has fingerprints.
Sometimes freedom looks like a door that stays closed.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like deleting a number while your hands are shaking.
Sometimes obedience feels like grief before it feels like freedom.
That is part of the force of Jesus’ metaphor.
An eye is valuable.
A hand is useful.
Jesus deliberately chooses things a person would hate to lose.
Why?
Because following Christ may require surrendering something you genuinely value when keeping it continually leads you toward destruction.
There are things you can love and still need to leave.
There are people you can miss and still not call again.
There are environments you can enjoy and still never enter again.
There are habits that once comforted you that cannot accompany you where Christ is leading you.
Some doors need prayer.
Others need locks.
Some temptations need Scripture.
Others need Scripture and a blocked number.
Sometimes we pray, “Lord, deliver me from temptation,” while preserving five different ways for temptation to contact us.
Then we call the cycle mysterious.
Jesus is painfully practical.
If it repeatedly causes you to stumble, stop treating access to it as sacred.
But there is another danger here.
Someone carrying crushing shame can hear Matthew 5 and conclude:
“God must hate me.”
No.
The warning itself reveals that eternity matters.
Christ speaks urgently because sin matters, judgment matters, and people matter.
Biblical conviction says:
Come out of hiding and come to Christ.
Condemnation whispers:
Hide from Christ until you have repaired yourself.
Those are not the same message.
Think about Peter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
At the moment when loyalty became costly, the disciple who had spoken so confidently collapsed spectacularly.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine replaying the sound of your own voice:
“I do not know the man.”
But Peter's scandal was not the final chapter.
The risen Christ met him again.
Restored him.
Commissioned him.
Grace did not pretend the denial never happened.
Grace rewrote what happened next.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not because sin was imaginary.
Not because repentance became unnecessary.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
But because failure does not possess greater authority than Jesus Christ.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe it lives entirely behind your ribs.
Jesus sees that too.
And the same Christ who says, “Throw away what makes you stumble,” is the Christ who receives sinners who turn to Him.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“Was Jesus literally telling me to tear out my eye?”
Perhaps the question is:
What am I unwilling to tear out of my life even though I know it keeps tearing my life apart?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
What came to mind before you started making excuses?
A name?
An app?
A website?
A habit?
A relationship?
A hidden folder?
A bottle?
A conversation?
A place?
An ambition?
A grudge?
An image?
An identity built around being desired, admired, wealthy, powerful, noticed, or needed?
What did your heart immediately defend?
Maybe that is where the conversation with Jesus needs to begin.
Not with a knife against your body.
With honesty before God.
“Jesus, I have been protecting what is poisoning me.”
That confession can become the beginning of freedom.
And if you fall again, do not turn another failure into permission to surrender completely.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get help.
Bring darkness into the light.
Take concrete steps.
Keep fighting.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the reason chains no longer have to define you.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who never struggled.
We are people who desperately need Christ.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because temptation has a way of making yesterday's convictions strangely difficult to remember.
Not as proof that you have everything together.
Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God's favor.
But supporting Christian ministry can be one practical way of helping biblical resources reach more people.
But before you leave this page, go back to the question.
Not somebody else's eye.
Not somebody else's hand.
Not somebody else's scandal.
Yours.
What are you protecting that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
You do not need to destroy your body.
Christ is calling you to stop making peace with the thing destroying you.
Bring it into the light.
Cut off its access.
Run toward Jesus.
And when shame tells you that your worst chapter has already written your ending, look toward the cross and the empty tomb.
Because the hands of Christ are still better authors than your failures.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived here, but when you surrender the pen to Jesus, it does not get to write your final sentence.
